evidence_quotes.quote: The collectivized SGAB undertook a number of initiatives leading to the improvement of the access to water by the citizens such as the rationalization of water pricing or the increase of the amount of water available for ﬂats after the application of hygienist principles.
Our research has been based on a partial access to SGAB archives, which permitted us to examine the company’s correspondence between 1936 and 1940 (12 boxes, some 8000 documents).

Third, the water bill was split between the landlord who would pay a ﬁxed fee based on the minimum consumption set by the municipal health service, and the tenant who would pay consumption in excess of that minimum amount. All minimums were to be revised according to the number of rooms and water points. In those cases where the 1930 law was not complied with, the amount of water delivered to the ﬂat was automatically increased.

After the breakup of the war the anarchist neighborhood association took over the spring and transferred its ownership to the SGAB. In return, the company installed piped water in many houses, thus increasing the number of customers.
Nevertheless, perhaps the most important change, also quietly accepted after the war, was the general increase of minimum quantities of water per ﬂat.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household piped water supply access, tariffs, metering, minimum water provision to rented flats, and service continuity in Barcelona (including working-class districts and slums).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under both readings. Plain wording: examines institutional/governance changes (worker collectivization of the private water utility SGAB) and municipal regulatory decrees (the 1930 Municipal Public Health decree and 1932 amendments, plus 1938 regional wartime water orders). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing household water access, including utility ownership/property regime (worker-collectivized utility vs private corporation), tariff and cost-recovery rules (unifying city-wide tariffs at 40 cents/m3, abolishing fixed meter fees, and splitting bills between landlords paying a fixed fee for statutory minimum volumes and tenants paying excess consumption), tenure/contracting enforcement (unilaterally enforcing the 1930 ordinance's minimum per-flat supply thresholds previously evaded by landlords bundling cistern water into rent, and cancelling nineteenth-century perpetuity contracts), and wartime use restrictions and regulated price increases.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative historical and socio-legal empirical case study using primary archival sources (12 boxes / approximately 8,000 documents of SGAB correspondence from 1936-1940, SGAB annual reports, official administrative diaries, and contemporary press clips) supplemented by two interviews with key former SGAB workers. Per review rules, qualitative empirical studies are eligible regardless of lack of a quantitative effect estimate.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes relevant to household water quantity delivered (automatic increases in minimum flat water allocations, a 10,000 m3 city consumption increase by early 1937, and a 15% increase in water supplied to the city by 1939), new piped household connections (in the working-class Trinitat neighborhood), tariff levels and bill non-payment rates (rising to >80% after rent suspension), and wartime service continuity/reliability.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (the collectivized utility SGAB and urban households, landlords, and tenants in Barcelona, 1936-1939), exposure (worker collectivization and associated tariff, metering, billing-split, contract-termination, and minimum-supply enforcement rules), outcomes (water quantity delivered per flat and city-wide, new piped connections, tariff affordability/non-payment, and supply continuity), and study design (historical archival and interview-based qualitative case study) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative historical case study (archival document analysis and key-informant interviews)
population_and_sample: Urban water utility Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona (SGAB) and urban households, tenants, and landlords in Barcelona, Spain (1936-1939; city population ~1,200,000); empirical data drawn from 12 archival boxes (~8,000 correspondence documents from 1936-1940), utility annual reports, official diaries, press archives, and 2 interviews with former SGAB workers.
exposure: Worker collectivization of the Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona (SGAB, 1936-1939) and its rule-type tariff, contracting, and regulatory reforms: city-wide tariff unification (40 cents/m3, later 70 cents/m3 in 1938), abolition of fixed meter fees, mandatory landlord meter purchase, splitting water bills between landlords (fixed fee for statutory minimum volume) and tenants (excess volume), unilateral enforcement of the 1930 Municipal Public Health decree minimum supply thresholds per flat, and termination of perpetuity water contracts.
outcome: Household piped water connections (e.g., new piped connections in the Trinitat working-class neighborhood), minimum water quantities delivered per flat and total municipal supply (+10,000 m3 in early 1937; +15% city supply by 1939), tariff levels and bill non-payment rates (rising to >80% following rent suspension), and service continuity under wartime power cutoffs and air raids.
rationale: This full-text English-language empirical historical case study meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Using primary utility archives (~8,000 documents) and key-informant worker interviews, it examines how a shift in utility property/governance regime (worker collectivization of Barcelona's private water utility SGAB) and concrete rule-type legal/administrative mechanisms—city-wide tariff unification, abolition of fixed meter charges, splitting water bills between landlords and tenants, cancelling perpetuity contracts, and unilaterally enforcing the 1930 Municipal Public Health decree's minimum per-flat supply thresholds previously resisted by landlords—affected household piped water connections, minimum per-flat water quantities delivered, city-wide water supply, bill non-payment, and wartime service continuity. Qualitative socio-legal/historical empirical studies with identifiable primary data and methods are eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.
